analytic.title: How Fast Can a BDI Agent Respond?

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: It is very important to know how fast a BDI agent can react to and process incoming event sequences if we want to apply such autonomous agents into time-sensitive applications like the Close-In weapon system in air-carriers. In [15], we proposed an analysis method for traditional sequential agents. In this paper we extend the theoretical analysis method to parallel BDI agents. Our method can estimate the average response time using the average attributes of a sequence of events based on probability and queueing theory. The simulation experiments show that our theoretical analysis method is effective. We also show by an experiment that an agent that dynamically allocates its computational time resources perform better than one that does not. Thus, the theoretical method suggests a way to quickly estimate the performance of an agent if the average attributes of the incoming event sequence are known in advance. Such an analysis of average response time can definitely benefit constructing more efficient BDI agents that situate in time-sensitive environments.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The BDI (belief-desire-intention) model is widely accepted as agent architecture to support goal oriented behaviour. It provides a folk psychological way by simulating the human way of decision making. The mental attitudes of belief, desire and intention represent the information, motivational, and deliberative states of the agent respectively [4], [11]. The processing of an event inside a BDI agent is in a sequential way: firstly detect action, then deliberate action, and finally execute action. This popular approach has been used in many agent systems [1], [2], [6], [8], [13]. During the running of a BDI agent, the time to process events can be recorded and analyzed to evaluate the responsiveness of the agent.

How to rationally allocate time resources to the three actions (detect, deliberate and execute) in a BDI agent is a big problem when designing the agent. A defective mechanism for BDI agent can cause low responsiveness and waste of resources in the agent [10], [12]. Low responsiveness could lead to disastrous results in real applications.

For example, a BDI agent system for realizing the Close-In Weapon System (CIWS) on an aircraft carrier needs to detect and destroy incoming nuclear anti-ship missiles and other menaces as soon as possible. The weapon system fires bullets on possible paths of missiles. Once a missile changes its path suddenly, the system needs to immediately response to the new situation. It might be too late to modulate the agent after problem happens in such a real application. Thus it would be helpful if the responsiveness of the agent with a designed mechanism could be known before the agent is put into practice. Unfortunately, currently few investigations have been carried out to predict the responsiveness of an agent although it is so important in any time-sensitive environment like that of the CIWS in aircraft carriers.

Simulation is a way to predict the performace of a BDI agent before it is implemented in real application. A sequence of events with attributes, like priorities and amounts of time which are needed in the three processes (detect, deliberate and execute) of the agent, are the inputs to the agent at designed insertion time. After receiving an event, the agent spends time on the event according to the attributes. The time that the agent spends in processing of the event can be recorded. Thus, the average response time for a sequence of events can be calculated. For different environments, event sequences with different attributes could be constructed. Then the responsiveness of the agent in such environments can be revealed through simulation experiments with the sequences.

In this paper, we will first introduce how event sequences are designed in our simulation experiments. Then we show a theoretical analysis of the agent when processing a sequence of events. The analysis is carried out in a way as queueing network [5], [9]. Queueing theory enables mathematical analysis of several performance measures including the average waiting time in the queues of a system, the number of tasks waiting or receiving service and the probability of encountering the system in certain states. An application can be seen as to reduce waiting times in hospitals [7]. In our analysis, the attributes of an incoming sequence of events are known in advance. Then the average waiting time for detection, deliberations (A deliberation is defined as the process to deliberate about a goal and generate an intention) and intentions in the queues will be analyzed. This provides an alternative way to estimate the responsiveness of agents without performing simulation experiments. We already showed our analysis of the traditional sequential BDI agent in [15]. We will extend the analysis to parallel BDI agent, which is a model by parallelizing the three actions of traditional BDI agents [14]. It is stated that the responsiveness of BDI agents is greatly improved after using multiple parallel running processors. In the following, traditional BDI agents are referred to as sequential BDI agents. The analysis result of parallel BDI agent is gotten based on the result of sequential BDI agent.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the queueing networks for BDI agents and simulation experiment design. Then the theoretical analyses method of average waiting time in sequential BDI agents and parallel BDI agents are developed in Sections III and IV, respectively. Section V compares the results of the theoretic analysis with that of the simulation. Accordingly, a way to design sequential BDI agents with the best performance is discussed in Section VI. Finally Section VII concludes the paper and point out the direction of further research based on this work.

div.head: II. PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: In this section, firstly the processing inside sequential BDI agent and parallel BDI agent are modeled in the form of queueing networks. Then the design of event sequences for the networks is discussed. Finally, we introduce the performance marks for the agents, which will be analyzed in following sections.

div.head: A. Basic models
div.p: The processing inside BDI agents can be seen as open queueing networks. Events enter the agents and are processed by the agent as shown in Figure 1.

As shown in Figure 1(a), a sequential BDI agent's running consists of three cyclic actions: detect, deliberate and execute. An incoming event is saved in the event queue when the event occurs. In the agent, when it is the turn for detect action, the events are fetched and organized as deliberations in the deliberation queue. When it is the turn for deliberate action, the agent will deliberate about the events in the deliberation queue and save the generated intentions in the intention queue. Finally, the intentions in the intention queue will be executed when it is the turn for execute action. The three actions are repeated in a cyclical way.

In a parallel BDI agent as shown in Figure 1(b), the incoming events are processed by several processors, which run in parallel. The detect action receives new event and organizes it in the deliberation queue. It is assumed that this can be completed before next event comes because the detect processor is always running to receive new events. So there is no event queue here. Just 1 processor is sufficient for the detect action. Similarly, the deliberate and execute processors also run in parallel. The lengths of all the queues in Figure 1 are infinite.

div.head: B. Simulation experiment design
div.p: In the simulation, we assume that the smallest time unit is 1 and the system clock starts from 0. A sequence of events is set up. The attributes of an event include:
• Priority : importance of the event.
• Insertion time: the time when the event occurs.

• S 1 : detection time. Service time needed to detect and organize the event to generate a deliberation. We assume it equals to the smallest time unit of 1. • S 2 : deliberation time. Service time needed to complete the deliberation. • S 3 : execution time. Service time needed to execute the intention. The smallest interval between two events is 1. The priority value of an event is used to decide the importance of the intention which is generated according to the event. The priority value has no effect on detect or deliberate actions because the agent cannot decide the importance of an event before the deliberation about the event is accomplished. The generated intention is assigned with the priority value. An intention with bigger priority value should be executed earlier. In this paper, the priorities of events are uniformly distributed in [1, P max ] where P max is the maximum priority value.

In experiments, the operations of BDI agents are simulated. A sequential BDI agent must allocate its computation resources to the three actions rationally. In the following experiments and analysis, we will adopt the "fixed time" allocation mechanism as used in Touringmachines [3]. That is each action is assigned with fixed computation time. When the time for one action is used up, the next action will start. A little improvement is that a task (deliberation / intention) can be suspended and resumed in next cycle if the current remaining time is not sufficient for completing the task. In Touringmachines, the remaining time will be wasted if it is not big enough to complete a task.
Then, for a sequential BDI agent, we define the following variables:
• t 1 : time allocated for detect action.
• t 2 : time allocated for deliberate action.
• t 3 : time allocated for execute action.
div.formula: • t = t 1 + t 2 + t 3 : total time in a cycle. • R 2 = t2 t : the ratio of deliberate time in a cycle. • R 3 = t3

div.head: C. Performance marks
div.p: The agent performance is evaluated by the Average Response Time (ART) for the events in a sequence. Response time for an event is defined as the period between the time that the event is inserted and the time that the response to the event is completed. A smaller ART indicates that the agent can process the events quicker. Our objective is to estimate the ART of the agent in an environment which is specified by a sequence of events.
Given the sequence of events, we have the following values:
• N : number of events in the sequence.
• interval: average length of intervals between events.
• S 1 : average detection time of the events.
• S 2 : average deliberation time of the events.
• S 3 : average execution time of the events. Then the ART can be calculated by:
div.formula: ART = W T 1 + S 1 + W T 2 + S 2 + W T 3 + S 3 (1)
div.p: where W T 1 is average waiting time between an event occurs and it gets detected; W T 2 is average waiting time between a deliberation is inserted to the deliberation queue and it gets serviced; and W T 3 is average waiting time between an intention is inserted to the intention queue and it gets executed.

After the values of average waiting time are estimated, the ART can be calculated by combining them with the values of average service time. We will analyze the values of average waiting time in next two sections.

div.p: V. EXPERIMENTS
In order to see how closely these formulas can approximate the real performance of the agents, we make the following comparison experiments.

The time allocation mechanism for the sequential BDI agent is t 1 = 1, t 2 = 2, and t 3 = 4. Thus according to formula (2), the estimated W T 1 is 3. The parallel BDI agent consists of 1 deliberate processor and 1 execute processor.
A total number of N=1000 events will be created. The detection time of all events is 1 time unit. The priority value is selected randomly from 1 to 5.

In the following we will design different settings of experiments with different events deliberation time, execution time and intervals. The statistics collected from simulation experiments will be compared to the values estimated by using the formulas in previous analysis.

div.head: A. Experiment 1: Events with same deliberation time, execution time and fixed intervals
div.p: In this experiment, all the events are with same deliberation time 2 and execution time 4. The intervals between events are a fixed value. We designed five sequences of events with different intervals (1, 2, 4, 7, and 10). The sequences are input to the agents separately.

The average times gotten from analysis and simulation are shown in Table I. From the table, we can see that in this case, the formulas in analysis are quite good to estimate the real ART. When the fixed interval is 7, for the sequential agent, all events will be inserted exactly before a new cycle is started and detected in next time unit. Thus the events can be detected in next time units and waiting time for detection is 1. The response time for every event is 8.

div.head: B. Experiment 2: Events with random deliberation time and execution time, fixed intervals
div.p: In this case, the deliberation time of the events is chosen randomly in-between 1 and 3. The execution time of the intentions is chosen randomly in-between 1 and 7. The intervals are fixed. We still design 5 sequences. The results for the new sequences are shown in Table II.

When the fixed interval is 4, it is expected that the parallel agent will execute new intention immediately because S 3 is 3.9. However, in simulation, an intention with low priority value and large execution time may be suspended by later intentions with higher priority values for a long time if the agent cannot deal with it immediately. So the W T 3 from simulation is quite large (i.e., 16.25). When the fixed interval is 7, the sequential agent is expected to deal with the new event immediately after it is detected since the average time needed to process an event is around 7 (S 1 + S 2 + S 3 = 7.05 in this case). However, the deliberation about an event with deliberation time of 3 must be performed in 2 cycles considering t 2 = 2. Due to this, many deliberations about events cannot be processed in the same cycles as the events occur. This induces a bigger W T 2 (i.e., 23) in simulation than the expected W T 2 (i.e., 0). For the similar reason, W T 3 from simulation is also larger than the value from analysis.

div.head: C. Experiment 3: Events with same deliberation time and execution time, random intervals
div.p: In this case, all events have same deliberation time 2 and execution time 4. The intervals between events will be chosen randomly in-between 1 and the maxmum interval. We design 4 sequences with expected average intervals as 2, 4, 7, and 10. The maximum interval are 3, 7, 13, and 19, respectively. Then the results are shown in Table III. It is shown in the table that the differences between the results from analysis and simulation are smaller than in last case. The randomness of intervals is the reason for the differences. For example, when the average interval is 4.06, by analysis, because S 3 ≤ interval, the parallel agent is expected to finish executing an intention in the cycle in which the event occurs. However, many intervals ( 37 ≈ 43%) are smaller than 4 and two or more events may occur in a single cycle. Thus the parallel agent cannot finish executing two crowded events with interval smaller than 4 in expected time. This produces a bigger ART (i.e., 34.38) than ART (i.e., 7) from analysis.

div.head: D. Experiment 4: Events with random deliberation time, execution time, and intervals
div.p: In this case, all the variables will be chosen randomly as in previous experiments. The results are shown in Table IV. The differences are larger than in the last 2 cases due to a bigger extent of randomness. From the experiments, we can see that the analysis can provide quite good estimations when interval is smaller than the total time in a cycle of the sequential agent. However, when interval is bigger than the total time in a cycle, the results from analysis are normally too optimistic compared to the results from simulation. The differences are noticeable when interval is closer to the total time in a cycle. It is because the analysis is made based on the average attributes of the events. In simulation, the waiting time is affected by the attributes of single events. Simple average values cannot represent the characteristics of the events in the sequence in a precise way.

div.head: VI. DISCUSSION
div.p: In order to design an effective BDI agent, it is preferred to have smaller ART . The values of the average waiting time should be smaller. The agent should be able to process all the incoming events in a cycle. So from the analysis, we have the conditions:

div.p: From formula (7), a smaller t 2 will help decrease W T 3 . Considering the formula (3), it is preferred that t ≤ interval. Formula (2) shows that if t 2 and t 3 are decided, a bigger t 1 can help decrease W T 1 . Thus a mechanism to allocate resources is:
We can see that the mechanism will ensure that the sequential BDI agent processes an event in a cycle. At the same time, the agent can spend as much time as possible on detecting.

In order to test the effectiveness of the prediction method, we make an experiment to compare the performance of the agent with or without the mechanism to dynamically allocate resources. In the experiment, we design 300 events. For the first 100 events, the average interval is 7, S 2 is randomly selected from [1,3], and S 3 is randomly selected from [1,7]. For the second 100 events, the average interval is 9, S 2 is randomly selected from [1,3], and S 3 is randomly selected from [1,9]. For the third 100 events, the average interval is 5, S 2 is randomly selected from [1,3], and S 3 is randomly selected from [1,5]. We designed 4 kinds of BDI agents. The first three BDI agents are working with fixed resource allocation schema.While the last agent will modulate its resource allocation dynamically. As a result, for the first 100 events, its resource allocation schema is t 1 =1, t 2 =2, and t 3 =4. For the second 100 events, the schema is t 1 =1, t 2 =2, and t 3 =5. And for the last 100 events, the schema is t 1 =1, t 2 =2, and t 3 =3. The average waiting time for the 4 agents is shown in Table 5. Obviously, the last agent is able to work more effectively than the first three agents. For example, the ART of agent 4 is 87.433/73.667 ≈ 1.187 times faster than the ART of agent 2. This shows that the idea to dynamically allocate resources to the BDI agent can improve the efficiency of the BID agent in dynamic environments.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we present two ways for predicting the responsiveness of BDI agents, simulation and theoretical analysis. By analysis, if the basic information of the event sequence and the settings of a BDI agent are known, the average response time can be estimated using the formulae. The results of the analysis provide a quick way to estimate the agent performance without making simulation experiments. The comparison of results from simulation and analysis shows that the performances can be estimated well by analysis if the average interval between events is smaller than the total time in a cycle.

The main contribution of this paper is to provide a theoretical analysis to estimate the responsiveness of BDI agents before the agents are implemented in real applications. The predicted average response time may help modulate the allocation mechanism of a BDI agent for better performance.
In another case, it can help select one agent which has best performance for a specific environment among several BDI agents.

In future research, we will concentrate on the analysis when an agent is expected to have sufficient time to process events immediately. The analysis will be made based on the unique characteristics of single events, for example, the distribution function of the intervals and how the deliberation and execution time are decided. It is expected to give more precise estimations for such sequences.
